question: Will Squamish property taxes go up in 2027?
short: Will Squamish property taxes go up in 2027?
answer: Very likely, yes. District staff's draft 2027 budget needs 10.4% more property tax revenue than 2026. That works out to about $342 more for an average home, before any extra items council decides to add. The new council still has to approve the plan, and the final number is not set yet.

p.t: Staff presented the General Fund operating budget to council on September 29, 2026. The base plan needs 10.4% more property tax revenue in 2027 than in 2026. Staff say that is about $342 more for the average home, measured against an average 2026 municipal tax of $3,294.

That 10.4% does not include extra services that were still waiting on council approval. Staff priced those at another 1.7% (about $56 for an average home) for added service and up to 1.2% for one time projects. At the September 29 meeting, council kept most of the extra services but cut two items worth $123,000 and $58,000, and sent a $580,000 community safety package back for more work. No updated total has been published.

after.t: This is the increase in the total tax the District collects, not a promise about your own bill. Your bill depends on how your assessment changed compared with others in your neighbourhood and property class.

p.t: Staff list the main costs. Wages and benefits under existing union and staff contracts add 2.2%. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police contract adds 1.1%. Higher debt payments, mostly for the new Public Works Facility, add 1.8%. Transit adds 0.5%, and the Cheekye debris flow barrier reserves add 0.5%.

Staff also kept setting aside $7.2 million, equal to the general tax paid by a single large business, for one time spending like capital projects instead of day to day operations. This follows the District's tax policy of not relying on one taxpayer for ongoing costs.

Squamish adopted its first ten year financial plan (2026 to 2035) on January 13, 2026. That plan predicted a 13.0% tax revenue increase for 2027 and 12.9% for 2028. The new draft is lower for 2027, but staff still forecast 12.7% for 2028 and 7.9% for 2029.

after.t: Staff say the 2028 jump comes from new police positions that were partly covered by a reserve fund until now, plus more borrowing for the Mamquam Bridge deck, the Xwu'nekw Park sea dike and Squamish River dike raising.

sections.h: Water, sewer and garbage fees for 2027

p.t: Utility fees are billed separately from property tax. Staff recommended a 1.8% rise for water and 8.8% for sewer, and proposed 10.3% for curbside garbage.
On September 22, 2026, council approved water at 1.8% and sewer at 8.8%, and lowered the garbage increase to 8.3%. These rates still need to go into the fees bylaw before they take effect.

Council held budget workshops on September 8, September 22, September 29 and October 6, 2026. The new council took office on November 3. The District says a workshop to introduce the plan to the new council and a public information night are coming, but the dates had not been posted as of November 9.

The 2026 plan was adopted in January, so the final 2027 number may not come until the new council votes in the coming weeks. Tax rates themselves are set in the spring, after BC Assessment releases its revised roll.

The District posts every budget report and its online budget book on Let's Talk Squamish, where you can answer its questions about what matters most to you. You can also email budgetfeedback@squamish.ca at any time. Feedback goes to the new council, and the District will publish a What We Heard report.

faq: Are property taxes going up in 2027 in Squamish?
Almost certainly. The draft budget needs at least 10.4% more property tax revenue than 2026, about $342 for an average home, before extra items council adds. Council has not adopted it yet.
How much did taxes go up in 2026 and 2025?
The 2026 increase was 12.8%, adopted January 13, 2026. The 2025 increase was 12.5%.
Will my own tax bill go up by exactly 10.4%?

Not necessarily. That number is the increase in total tax collected. Your bill depends on how your assessment changed compared with others in your property class. New construction also spreads the cost over more properties.
When will the 2027 budget be final?
The District has not posted the date yet. The new council has to vote on the financial plan, and tax rates are set in the spring of 2027.
How can I give input on the 2027 budget?
Use letstalksquamish.ca/budget-2027, email budgetfeedback@squamish.ca, or attend the public information night once its date is announced.

question: Why did Squamish property taxes go up 12.8%?
short: Why Squamish property taxes went up 12.8%
answer: The District of Squamish raised the property tax money it collects to run the town by 12.8% for 2026, to $56.1 million. Most of the increase paid for costs it was already committed to, such as staff wages and benefits, RCMP policing, transit, inflation and debt on projects already approved. Council debated the budget in late 2025 and adopted it unanimously on January 13, 2026.

p.t: Both dates come up. Council worked on the budget in late 2025 and adopted the 2026 to 2035 financial plan on January 13, 2026, so the 12.8% increase is on 2026 tax bills. The year before, 2025, taxes for operations went up 12.5%.

sections.h: What it cost a typical property

p.t: The District's 2026 figures for the municipal part of the tax bill. School and regional district taxes are extra.

after.t: Earlier estimates said about $382 or $389 more for the average home. Those were drafts; the figures above are from April 2026, after tax rates were set.

p.t: When staff presented the draft budget on December 9, 2025, it was a 13.1% increase. They broke it down like this (the final increase was 12.8%):

list: About 7.7 points: costs already committed, such as labour and benefit contracts, policing, transit, inflation and debt payments on approved projects.
About 2.9 points: keeping services at their current level, including fire services and transit.
About 2.4 points: money set aside to repair and replace roads, pipes and buildings.
The rest: new or one time projects and community grants.

after.t: Staff said most of the increase came from costs the District could not avoid, not new services. The District's tax notice also lists growing RCMP and fire costs, new housing duties from the Province, debt for new facilities, and building reserves ($25.1 million in 2026).
Armand Hurford, mayor at the time, called the town's shortage of facilities one of the main drivers.

p.t: Utility fees are billed separately. For 2026, sewer (wastewater) fees went up 7.2%, water 1.8% and garbage collection 5.2%.

sections.h: Why the total tax collected rose more than 12.8%

p.t: In spring 2026 the District collected $5.8 million more than planned from Woodfibre LNG, after the plant's assessment jumped. Council put that money into reserves for building projects instead of daily operations, so it did not lower anyone's bill. With it, total municipal taxes for 2026 were $61.9 million.

The 10 year plan expects increases of about 13% in 2027 and 12.9% in 2028, mostly for RCMP contracts, debt payments and more fire staff and transit. Staff's first draft for 2027, shown in September 2026, starts at 10.4% before new items. The new council decides the 2027 budget over the winter.

faq: How much did Squamish property taxes go up in 2026?
The money the District collects for operations went up 12.8%, to $56.1 million. For the average single family home, the municipal part of the bill went up $520, to $4,466.
Why did Squamish raise property taxes so much?

Mostly for costs it was already committed to: wages and benefits, RCMP policing, transit, inflation and debt on approved projects. Smaller parts went to keeping fire and transit service levels and to reserves for repairing roads, pipes and buildings.
Did Woodfibre LNG's taxes lower the increase?
No. The extra $5.8 million from Woodfibre in 2026 went into reserves for building projects, not daily operations.

question: How much does Squamish depend on Woodfibre LNG's taxes?
short: How much Squamish depends on Woodfibre LNG's taxes
answer: Woodfibre LNG paid about 12% of the District of Squamish's municipal property taxes in 2026, up from 3% in 2025, as the plant's assessed value rose while it was built. It is the town's only major industry property. The District puts that extra money into reserves rather than daily operations, so the operating budget does not depend on it.

p.t: Municipal property taxes only, from the District's tax rate reports.

after.t: The District's Woodfibre page says the company paid $7.7 million in 2026. The tax rate report shows $7.24 million levied on its property. Neither explains the difference.

p.t: The plant's assessed value rose 391% from 2025 to 2026 as construction went on, from $11.8 million to $57.9 million. The tax rate stayed the same: $125 for every $1,000 of assessed value for major industry, set in 2024 when Squamish had no property in that class.

For comparison, the District says the average major industry rate in B.C. communities that have one was $31 per $1,000 in 2026. When the pulp mill closed in 2006, the rate on that site was $58 per $1,000 and the mill paid about 16% of the town's municipal taxes.

sections.h: What the District does with it

p.t: District staff wrote that it is best practice not to rely on revenue from a single large business to fund ongoing operations. So the District puts Woodfibre money above what it planned for into reserves for one time spending: $1.5 million in 2025 and $5.8 million in 2026.

sections.h: The rejected deal and the court cases

p.t: Woodfibre has three legal cases against the District over its 2025 and 2026 taxes and other matters. In 2026 the District negotiated a 10 year deal worth at least $142 million: fixed payments of $117 million into a capital reserve, plus municipal taxes capped at $2.5 million a year (rising with inflation from 2028). The deal would have ended the court cases.

Council rejected it 5 to 2 on September 22, 2026. Councillors Andersen and French voted for the deal. So regular property taxation continues and the court cases go ahead. District staff said regular taxes could end up higher or lower than the deal.
The new council sets the 2027 tax rates, including the major industry rate, in spring 2027. It could also try to negotiate a new agreement.

faq: How much tax does Woodfibre LNG pay Squamish?
About $7.2 million in municipal property taxes in 2026 (the District's Woodfibre page says $7.7 million), up from $1.47 million in 2025.
What share of Squamish's taxes comes from Woodfibre LNG?
About 12% of municipal property taxes in 2026, up from 3% in 2025.
Does Squamish's budget depend on Woodfibre LNG?
The District says it is best practice not to rely on one large business for ongoing operations, so it puts Woodfibre money above plan into reserves for one time spending instead.
